newsitem.title: GERMANY: TIETMEYER - FOREX CRITERIA CRUCIAL FOR STABLE EMU.
newsitem.headline: TIETMEYER - FOREX CRITERIA CRUCIAL FOR STABLE EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said on Tuesday that nations must fulfil all entry criteria, including the currency requirement, in order to ensure the currency union will be stable.

"In the interest of a stable currency union all criteria must be fulfilled, this also includes the foreign exchange rate criteria and that a nation needs to be a member of the exchange rate mechanism without a problem," Tietmeyer told a group of bankers.

In a speech prepared for delivery here, Tietmeyer warned, "a nation that cannot keep its exchange rate in the close range of a set rate, obviously has difficulties in keeping its economy in step with those of other currency union candidates."

Tietmeyer, a fervent supporter of a strict interpretation of the entry criteria, added "this is the spirit of the currency criteria and this is true today just as it was when the Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1991."
Stressing that the German constitutional court ruled that the criteria must interpreted strictly, Tietmeyer said that his position does not reflect "narrow minded view" of the Bundesbank.
Tietmeyer said the European currency union needed a real deterrent against lax fiscal policies and urged policy-makers to adopt a tough stability pact.
"We need a real rule that acts as a deterrent against lax fiscal policies," Tietmeyer said.

Tietmeyer said progress on the stability pact -- which will trigger automatic sanctions against nations who stray in fiscal austerity -- was good but warned the European Commission's proposal on the pact did not go far enough.

"I hope that it will be possible to approach the Dublin results and to clarify the still unresolved details," Tietmeyer said, adding that the Commission proposal was not as firm as he had expected following talks in Dublin in September.
Tietmeyer, one of the staunchest supporters of a strict interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty criteria, also warned, "In no event may the currency union become a transfer union."
Tietmeyer warned nations against tailoring their finances in order to pass the entry test to Europe's currency union, saying such moves would undermine the new currency.
"I view certain beauty operations with worry as they are clearly designed to improve the finances for the appointed date," Tietmeyer said.
"One-time efforts are not appropriate to create the necessary trust in the Euro."
In a bid to be among the first group of nations to join the European currency union in 1999, several nations are using special one-off factors to adjust their finances.
France, for example, will be able to use funds from a transfer from France Telecom to reduce its budget deficit in 1997.
Tietmeyer warned confidence and trust in the new currency could be created only if the right nations enter the union.
"It is absolutely necessary that only nations with a convergent stability policy and sufficiently solid public finances can enter the currency union."
"A beautifully posed photograph on a sunny day does not set the stage for a good future," Tietmeyer said.

Tietmeyer, known as one of the staunchest supporters for a strict interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty criteria, also said "in the interest of a stable currency union, all criteria must be fulfilled."

There has been growing talk that nations may not need to meet all the criteria on stable currencies, low inflation and interest rates and low deficit and debt ratios to overall gross domestic product.
Tietmeyer stressed the importance of minimum reserves for a successful monetary policy but also raised hopes the central bank may ease the German reserve requirement again.

Weighing into a debate raging between commercial bankers and central bank officials about the need for minimum reserves, Tietmeyer said "Is the minimum reserve concept really necessary for monetary policy? In our view the answer is still Yes."
Banks in Germany are required to hold minimum reserves on short-term borrowings obtained from foreign banks or domestic non-banks in non-interest-bearing accounts at the central bank.
"A financial system's stability and a stable currency cannot be obtained for free," Tietmeyer warned in the speech prepared for delivery to a group of foreign bankers.
The Bundesbank says this helps it guide monetary policy but bankers complain the requirement only chips away at their international competitiveness.
At the moment the Bundesbank is the only central bank in Europe that has significant non-interest bearing minimum reserves.

While commercial bankers are lobbying for the concept to be scuttled by the future European Central Bank, Tietmeyer said they should not get their hopes up as central bankers generally favour the use of reserves.
"We do not rule out the fact that small changes can be made to the German system but we do think that our system is acceptable for Europe," Tietmeyer said.
EU nations have generally agreed to adopt minimum reserves in the currency union even though it has not yet been decided whether they should be interest bearing or non-interest bearing.
But Tietmeyer also raised hopes that the Bundesbank may consider easing the requirement by exempting so-called repo business from the requirement.
"The council is currently evaluating whether an exemption of securities repurchase agreements can be acceptable, I expect that a decision will be reached on this soon."

Currently the reserve level is two percent of sight and term deposits and 1.5 percent of savings deposits. Commerical banks say most repo business has moved abroad in order to escape the reserve requirement.
If repo transactions are exempted, commercial bankers maintain the Bundesbank will improve Germany's reputation as av financial centre and help bring lost business back.
Market speculation that the central bank will announce this step before the end of the year has been high.
--Svea Herbst-Bayliss, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
